newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-INDIA FEBRUARY MARKET STRATEGY-BY ING BARINGS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-INDIA FEBRUARY MARKET STRATEGY-BY ING BARINGS.

text.p: "The Market Will Soon Fall in Line With
Fundamentals," is a report on the Indian economy and stock markets by securities firm ING Barings.
NET FII INFLOWS ARE DISAPPOINTING:

The customary opportunistic buying by FIIs in December 1996, in anticipation of robust fresh asset allocations to emerging markets in January, has been the prime trigger apart from 'cheap' valuations for the bear market rally seen in the Indian stock market during the last two months.
Although FII buying has been good, aggressive selling by sceptical FIIs (in the rising markets during the last two months) has resulted in disappointing numbers for net buying.

It should be noted that net FII buying during December 1996-January 1997 has been barely US$200 millions (ie, down 50 percent YoY) although the market has been rallying for seven weeks now, compared to rallying for just one week in the corresponding period of the previous year.
THE INVESTORS' DILEMMA:
The reasons for the lacklustre level of net FII inflows are not hard to find. Unlike in the early 1990s, the underlying story has become very important for investors in emerging markets today.
There is also greater competition for foreign portfolio/direct investment, as a result of the opening up of several new emerging markets.

Moreover, the growth story in many of these markets (such as the Asian tigers) is showing signs of fatigue; only those markets which show clear signs of economic revival and corporate earnings growth are likely to receive allocations on a priority basis.

As a case in point, major flows this year (to date) have been to Eastern Europe, Russia and Latin America; Asia has fared rather poorly. We also believe that major emerging market allocations will depend on the course taken by the Dow Jones in 1QCY97.
Investors in the Indian stock market are at a crossroads.
They are undecided about the big picture as well as the earnings story; there are contradictory signals emanating from different quarters and no consensus seems to be emerging.

The macroeconomic view ranges from 'insignificant industrial slowdown' (the official view represented by the Central Statistical Organisation's data) and 'minor slowdown only in 1HFY3/97 followed by a turnaround' (held by a majority of investment bankers and the CMIE) to 'deep industrial slowdown bordering on a recession, with no apparent signs of a turnaround in the near future' (ING Barings).

On the corporate earnings front, there was near-consensus among investment banks (with the exception of ING Barings) a bare two months ago that growth would be 15-25 percent in FY3/97 and 20-25 percent in FY3/98.
However, several analysts have now downgraded FY3/97 estimates significantly (as the year draws to a close) and forecasts of growth for FY3/98 are maintained with apparent uneasiness.
However, we have consistently maintained that corporate India delivered its peak performance in FY3/96 and is unlikely to better this during FY3/97 or FY3/98.
The major reasons for our believing this are: demand fatigue, growing competition (both internal and external) and an unprecedented cost push in 1996 and 1997.
Investors are liable to be confused by the upside potential being projected for the Indian stock market, by a majority of investment banks.

The consensus Sensex (benchmark Bombay stocks index) target of 3800-3950 (for December 1997) is a mere 6-9 percent above current levels; hence, the potential currency risk of 8-10 percent and opportunity cost of 5.5-6.0 percent (gains possible from debt instruments) effectively send out 'stop buying' signals to FIIs!
ILLUSION OF GROWTH:
Undoubtedly, the industrial slowdown/revival is the most contentious issue at the moment.

Everyone (including government agencies, economists, corporates and analysts) acknowledged the existence of a slowdown in industrial production (in varying degrees) during 1Q-3QFY3/97 and predicted a revival thereafter.
However, it would seem that people are now 'wishing' that the worst is over; there is very little cogent evidence to prove the revival theory.
We feel that there are serious question marks in the arguments being put forth in support of an industrial turnaround.
We outline them here to provide a better understanding of this important issue:
** MYTH:
Bumper agricultural production will propel an industrial revival and economic growth in CY1997.
** REALITY:
An analysis of economic data over the last 20 years shows no correlation whatsoever between agricultural and industrial growth, with or without lag effects.
In fact, there have been several years with bumper agricultural production and dismal industrial growth!

Second, the quality and reliability of agricultural production data has been poor historically (due to the methodology employed); this is borne out by the repeated revisions in numbers by official agencies.
For instance, there was consensus (supported by official figures) throughout FY3/96 and up to September 1996, that India had a bumper crop in FY3/96 and agricultural growth was 2.4 percent.
However, revised numbers released subsequently showed negative growth for FY3/96 and projected higher growth for FY3/97.

Third, although agricultural supports 70 percent of the population, its contribution to GDP is only 30 percent, indicating that large sections of the agrarian population are not part of the market economy which drives industrial growth.
The 'bumper crop theory' is also undermined by the government's own food procurement programme, which has fallen short in absolute terms for three straight years.

We believe that growth in prices for farm produce (rather than production growth) determines the disposable surplus in the rural economy; the first two years of Dr Manmohan Singh's tenure were the best in this regard.

Similarly, the 'best-monsoon-year theory' is disturbingly at variance with the fact that reservoir levels in hydroelectric stations across the country are lower on a YoY basis and power generation by hydroelectric stations has been falling for two years in a row (down 17.5 percent YoY over July 1995-June 1996 and down 3.6 percent YoY over July 1996-November 1996).
In the last few years, with the advent of an omnipresent electronic media, a secular trend of growing consumerism is visible in rural India.
However, this should not be construed to be a function of increasing annual disposable income in the hands of farmers.
** MYTH:
Increased liquidity will drive industrial growth.
** REALITY:

The real liquidity crunch was faced by corporate India between October 1995 and March 1996. Thereafter, liquidity has been fairly easy and banks have been complaining that credit sanctions are under-utilised.

They cite a lack of genuine demand from standard assets and fears of rising NPAs (if they lend to existing and potential substandard assets) as the principal reasons for poor off-take of non-food credit.

Thus, poor banks advances are a symptom and not a cause of the continuing industrial slowdown. It has also been observed that the drop in PLR has not fuelled any significant credit demand, if one disregards the indirect financing of the oil pool deficit and quarterly interest dues clubbed with advances.
Leading bankers have gone on record to the effect that they did not foresee a major increase in credit off-take prior to a revival of both the primary capital market and of demand in the economy.
** MYTH:
The IIP growth numbers do not indicate any slowdown; on the contrary, industrial growth is robust, despite the poor show by the power sector.
** REALITY:

It must be conceded that the CSO (which compiles IIP data) has an increasingly difficult task as both the quality and the regular availability of industrial data are increasingly suspect, thanks to delicensing and other measures introduced with liberalisation.

Hence, we may have to depend more on primary drivers, such as growth in power generation, to assess industrial growth. We have observed through analysing data for the past 17 years, that growth in manufacturing (constituting 77 percent of the IIP) is usually 1.5 percent below the growth in power generation; however, major deviations from this norm began in FY3/96 and accelerated in FY3/97.

It is difficult to comprehend how a mere 2.8 percent growth in power generation during 1HFY3/97 (against a 15-year trend of 8.5 percent) can drive a robust 12.4 percent growth in manufacturing (against a 15-year trend of 7 percent); at no time in the past 15 years, would this meagre growth in power generation have produced more than a 2 percent increase in manufacturing.

It is also inconsistent with the fact that while power generation had grown at 11 percent in 1HFY3/96 (against 2.8 percent this year), the same growth of 12.5 percent had been achieved in manufacturing.
We believe that power is the major infrastructure sector driving the economy as a whole and has a very strong correlation with economic growth.
The policy document released recently by the Rakesh Mohan Committee. The India Infrastructure Report - Policy Imperatives for Growth and Welfare, suggests a rule of thumb:
Growth in power generation required =1.5 times economic growth desired.

By this measure too, the performance of the economy in the current years has been dismal. It may be mentioned in passing that the belief that captive power plants have substituted conventional power, is bogus.

First, captive power generation capacity consitutes a mere 10 percent of installed capacity in the country and is growing at 5-10 percent per annum. Second, consumption of fuel oils (which are used to fire the majority of generating sets) declined by 1.9 percent from March 1996 - November 1996 and by a further whopping 10 percent in December 1996.
** MYTH:
Falling real interest rates will drive industrial production and the stock market.
** REALITY:

Falling real interest rates on a term basis will have a pronounced effect on long-term investment but not on short-term production targets, which are primarily driven by demand for immediate consumption.

During the last two years, Indian corporates produced more, despite rising real interest rates, to cater for strong demand. However, it is erroneous to assume that flagging demand will be revived by a fall in real interest rates.
Moreover, long-term interest rates are unlikely to come down unless the fiscal deficit is reduced.
The causal relationship between falling real interest rates and a booming stock market is also far-fetched in the Indian context.

Stock investors in India are a very minute sub-set of bank deposit holding households; in the medium term, anticipated movements in stock prices are much more liable to determine fund flows into the stock market.
** MYTH:
Policy pronouncements according priority to infrastructure will lead to economic growth.
** REALITY:

It is true that investment in infrastructure development will lead to economic growth in the long term. However, very little investment has actually been made in it during the last four years since 'infrastructure' became a buzz word in the Indian economy.
Actual investment in the next two years is also not expected to be spectacular enough to trigger economic growth during that period.

In the meantime, the existing infrastructure is creaking and threatens to become a real bottleneck during the next 24 months. Ports are unable to handle large volume growth (exceptions are the new ports, eg, JNPT and Mangalore).

Capacity creation in the power sector has retarded significantly; installed generating capacity, which increased by a handsome 8.4 percent YoY in the late 1980s and a modest 5 percent YoY in the early 1990s is expected to be a mere 2.5 percent YoY during FY3/96-FY3/98, which will cap prospects of economic growth in the near future.
THE DARKEST HOUR IS BEFORE THE DAWN:
We believe that the deep industrial slowdown and evaporating corporate earnings being witnessed currently carry within them the seeds of burgeoning growth.

The creaking infrastructure, stagnating economy and bloated fiscal deficits of state and central governments will force a shift in focus - from the external reforms pursued in the last decade to internal reforms in the government.

We are of the opinion that due to the limited options available, a political consensus will be arrived at and major structural reforms will be implemented to restore fiscal discipline and woo foreign investment in earnest.
The battle being fought by Indian industry in the market place, along with the focusing and restructuring being undertaken, will result in the survival of the fittest.
This will lead to the emergence of a robust and healthy corporate India, ready to participate in the global economy in the years to come.
The Indian stock market and its constituents, eg, brokers, merchant bankers, investors and corporates, are undergoing a metamorphosis.

Automation, national reach, paperless trading and hedging instruments should see volumes in the market rise to the levels reached by the top three Asian markets (ex-Japan), over the next two-three years.

We believe PSEs are going to be the epicentre of the Indian stock market in future. They already have a 40 percent weighting in the Sensex and account for 33 percent of market capitalisation; 10 of the top 25 stocks traded are PSEs.
Systematic disinvetment and structural reforms can lead to substantial gains in productivity for large PSEs and this will be the driving force for the stock market in the future.
We believe that the government should go ahead with its disinvestment programme as quickly as possible, irrespective of domestic market conditions.
Shares of large Indian PSEs such as ONGC, IOC, MTNL, VSNL and BHEL can easily be placed abroad (though GDRs/ADRs), if the pricing is realistic and the underlying story is well-communicated.

In summary, we feel that an appreciation of the grim realities facing the Indian economy and corporates during CY1997 will bring the bear phase in the Indian stock market to an end; a sincere attempt at structural reforms will be sufficient to catapult it into a secular bull run.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters).
